about: WHO IMCI distance learning course (2014), Modules 1 and 2, in the Sudan national IMNCI wording. Each WHO section is cut into short lessons of one topic, with the same information as the WHO module, laid out as activities: step-by-step cards, flip cards, sorting, case stories and questions. Where the Sudan national booklet differs from WHO, the Sudan wording is used and a "Sudan national protocol" note says what WHO wrote. Chart booklet and recording form blocks are read live from the protocol. Video slots without a link show a placeholder; their narration scripts are in a separate file. Exercises start as drafts and open in the exercise manager.

sections.title: Module overview

read.text: See what Module 1 covers and where it fits in the IMCI process, then take the pre-test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text:
During the first face-to-face meeting you learned that the IMCI process always begins by checking all children for signs of serious illness.

In the sick child aged 2 months up to 5 years these are called general danger signs. In this module you will learn about these signs.
A sick child is 2 months up to 5 years of age. This means the child has not had his 5th birthday.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Note that the signs of serious illness for the sick young infant (under 2 months of age) are called general danger signs of serious disease. In Module 2 you will learn more about these signs and care for the sick young infant.
What you will be able to do

After you study this module, you will know how to:

  • Greet a caregiver and get important information for IMCI
  • Recognize general danger signs in a sick child
  • Provide urgent pre-referral treatment according to IMCI instructions
  • Refer a child when danger signs are present
How the module is organized

This module is divided into the following sections:

  1. Greet the caregiver
  2. Check for general danger signs
  3. Care when urgent referral is required
Where does this module fit in the IMCI process?
This module focuses on the first two steps in the IMCI process: greeting the caregiver and checking for general danger signs.

sections.title: Greeting the caregiver

read.text: Greet a caregiver well, use five good communication skills, and find out the four things you need before you assess.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Checking all sick children for general danger signs
read.caption: Watch this first. It walks through the whole section.

read.text: You will begin with a case study. This scene should be similar to situations that you see in your clinic. After it, you will learn how to (a) greet the caregiver and get important information about the child, and (b) check for general danger signs.

stages.text: Lebo's grandmother carries him into the clinic. Lebo does not look well. She has walked for one hour to the clinic. She tells you that she is also taking care of 4 other grandchildren. Lebo is her youngest grandchild and she is very worried about him. She says he is acting very unwell and has had a cough for 7 days.

The grandmother tells you as she sits down that Lebo's mother died 2 months ago. She says she does not know what caused the mother to die. Lebo's father works away and does not come home, only once every year or so. The grandmother is very worried about Lebo and very tired from her walking.

She tells you this is the first time she is bringing Lebo in to the clinic. You ask her how old Lebo is. She says he is 19 months old. You ask Lebo's grandmother her name. She tells you that her name is Nthabeleng.
stages.question: What is the first thing you do when Nthabeleng comes to the clinic?
options: Greet the caregiver and ask about the child
Refer Lebo to hospital at once
stages.explanation: The first step in the IMCI process is to greet the caregiver and ask about the child.

read.text: Why greet the caregiver?

Greeting the caregiver has two purposes:

  1. It makes a caregiver feel welcome in the clinic. Greeting and welcoming a caregiver is an important first step in building trust. It begins good and caring communication.
  2. It helps you gather important information about why the child is coming to the clinic.
Why is good communication with a caregiver important?

Caregivers can be very stressed and emotional when a child is ill. It is important for health workers to communicate concern and care for the child's health, and the family's situation. Good communication helps to reassure the caregiver that her child will receive good care.

When you treat the child's illness later in the visit, you will need to teach and advise the caregiver about caring for her sick child at home. Good communication and trust is essential here. It is important to have good communication with the caregiver from the beginning of the visit.

cards.back: Listen carefully to what the caregiver tells you. This shows you are taking her concerns seriously.
Use words the caregiver understands. If she does not understand what you ask her, she cannot give the information you need to assess and classify the child correctly.
Give the caregiver time to answer the questions. She might need time to decide if a sign you are asking about is present.
Ask additional questions when the caregiver is not sure about her answer. If she is not sure that a certain symptom or sign is present, ask additional questions. Help her make her answers clearer.
Praise the caregiver for what she is doing right. This will reinforce good practices.

read.text: What information do you gather during a greeting?
When you greet a caregiver you begin to ask important information about the child. This will help you in your assessment.

cards.back: The child's age determines which IMCI charts to use: the sick child or the young infant.

Why is the caregiver bringing the child to the clinic? Note the symptoms or health problems that are worrying them. If necessary, ask further detail: for example, how long the symptom has been present, or if it has been getting worse. You can also ask how she has been addressing the problem so far: this gives you background about previous care in the home, community, or other facilities.

Check if they are already recorded on the child's card. If not, weigh the child and measure his temperature later when you assess and classify the child's main symptoms. Do not undress or disturb the child now.
Is this the first visit for this problem, or a follow-up visit? These visits are different, so this is another important piece of information.

read.text:
ASK: first time coming to the clinic for this problem?

YES: INITIAL VISIT
ASSESS and CLASSIFY according to IMCI		NO: FOLLOW-UP VISIT
Give follow-up care according to IMCI

This is an initial visit if it is the child's first for this episode of illness. It is a follow-up visit if the child was seen a few days ago for the same problem. You will learn more about follow-up visits in later modules.

sections.title: Checking for general danger signs

read.text: Check every sick child for the general danger signs, one at a time, and say what you do when you find one.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: A child sleeps on her mother's lap. Is she lethargic?
options: Not necessarily: wake her and look
No, sleeping children are never sick
feedback: Sleeping is not the same as lethargic.
Right. Look at how she wakes and responds.
A sleeping child can be lethargic. You must look.

read.text: After greeting the caregiver, how do you begin assessing the child?

The first thing you check every sick child for is general danger signs. These signs are critically important. If Lebo shows any one of these signs, he is in danger. He needs urgent pre-referral treatment and immediate referral to the hospital.

A general danger sign is present if:

  • the child is not able to drink or breastfeed
  • the child vomits everything
  • the child has had more than one convulsion or prolonged convulsions, or is convulsing
  • the child is lethargic or unconscious
How will you check for a general danger sign?
You will ASK three questions and LOOK at the child. Open your chart booklet to the chart for general danger signs; it is shown here from the national protocol.

read.caption: Chart booklet: check for general danger signs (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.title: Checking for general danger signs, one step at a time

steps.title: ASK: Is the child able to drink or breastfeed?
steps.text: A child has the sign not able to drink or breastfeed if the child is not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink or breast milk. Make sure the caregiver understands the question. If she says the child is not able to drink or breastfeed, ask her to describe what happens when she offers the child something to drink: is the child able to take fluid into his mouth and swallow it? If you are not sure about her answer, ask her to offer the child a drink of clean water or breast milk, and look to see if the child swallows. A breastfed child may have difficulty sucking when his nose is blocked: clear it. If the child can breastfeed after the nose is cleared, the child does not have this danger sign.

steps.title: ASK: Does the child vomit everything?
steps.text: A child who is not able to hold anything down at all has the sign vomits everything: everything that goes down comes back up. He will not be able to hold down food, fluids, or oral drugs. A child who vomits several times but can hold down some fluids does not have this sign. Use words the caregiver understands and give her time to answer. If she is not sure, ask how often the child vomits, and whether he vomits each time he swallows food or fluids. If you are still not sure, ask her to offer the child a drink and see if he vomits.

steps.title: ASK: Has the child had convulsions?
steps.text: Ask if the child has had more than one convulsion, or prolonged convulsions, during this current illness. During a convulsion, the child's arms and legs stiffen because the muscles are contracting. The child may lose consciousness or not be able to respond to spoken directions. Use words the caregiver understands: she may call convulsions "fits" or "spasms".

steps.title: LOOK: Is the child lethargic or unconscious?
steps.text: A lethargic child is not awake and alert when she should be. She is drowsy and does not show interest in what is happening around her. Often the lethargic child does not look at the caregiver or watch your face when you talk, or will not respond if you clap or snap your fingers. The child may stare blankly. An unconscious child cannot be wakened: he does not respond when touched, shaken, or spoken to. Ask the caregiver if the child seems unusually sleepy or if she cannot wake him. Look to see if the child wakens when the caregiver talks to or shakes him, or when you clap your hands.

steps.title: LOOK: Is the child convulsing now?
steps.text: Look at the child. A child who is convulsing now has a general danger sign.

read.text: A breastfed child has a blocked nose and cannot suck. You clear his nose, and he breastfeeds well. Does he have the danger sign "not able to drink or breastfeed"?
read.answer: No. If the child can breastfeed after the nose is cleared, the child does not have the danger sign.

read.text: A child has vomited several times today, but he can hold down some fluids. Does he have the danger sign "vomits everything"?
read.answer: No. Only a child who cannot hold anything down at all has this sign.

read.text: What do you do if a child shows one or more general danger signs?

A child with a general danger sign has a serious problem. Most children with a general danger sign need urgent referral to hospital. The child might need lifesaving treatment with injectable antibiotics, oxygen, or other treatments that may not be available in your clinic.

If a child has a general danger sign, take IMMEDIATE ACTION: (1) complete the assessment immediately, because the child has a severe problem and there must be no delay in treatment; (2) provide urgent pre-referral treatment; (3) refer the child to hospital.
read.label: Immediate action

read.title: Does Lebo show any general danger signs?

stages.text: You ask if Lebo is able to drink or breastfeed, and Nthabeleng says, "No, not today, he is too tired." You try to give him some water from a cup but he is too weak and does not swallow. You ask Nthabeleng if Lebo is vomiting, and she says "no." You ask if Lebo is having convulsions, and Nthabeleng says "no."

You look at Lebo's condition. He is not paying attention to you or Nthabeleng as you talk, and only stares ahead. You snap your fingers in front of his face, but he does not look at the fingers. You ask Nthabeleng to bounce Lebo and speak to him, and when she says "Lebo! Lebo!" he does not look up at her.
stages.question: Which general danger signs does Lebo have?
options: Not able to drink, and lethargic
stages.explanation: Lebo is showing two general danger signs: he is unable to drink and he is lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.

stages.text: You tell Nthabeleng that Lebo needs further treatment at the hospital because he is unable to drink and is now acting very tired. You tell her it is very important that he go to the hospital right away, and that you will help arrange for her to get there. She looks very scared and asks if Lebo will die like his mother. She says this must be because of something she has done.
stages.question: What do you say to Nthabeleng?
options: Reassure her that it is because Lebo is sick, not because of her, and praise her for bringing him
Tell her there is nothing to worry about
Tell her she should have come sooner
stages.explanation: Affirm Nthabeleng: this is because Lebo is sick, not because of her actions. Explain that the treatment in the hospital will be able to help. Reassure her that she was a very good grandmother to bring Lebo, and very alert to notice that he was unwell.

stages.text: You tell her that you will start some immediate treatment now so that he can be stable during the journey to the hospital. You will then complete Lebo's assessment and decide what pre-referral treatment is necessary. He has a cough, so you must complete his classification for the cough to find the pre-referral treatment he needs. The lessons on urgent referral show you how.

read.text: How does the assessment continue after checking for general danger signs?

A child with any general danger sign needs URGENT attention. Complete the assessment and give any pre-referral treatment immediately so that referral is not delayed. You will learn much more about this in the following modules; your chart booklet walks you through the instructions.

read.title: What comes after the danger signs

cards.back: These are symptoms of the most common causes of illness and death in children under five: cough or difficult breathing (Module 3), diarrhoea (Module 4), and fever (Module 5). A number of illnesses, including pneumonia, malaria, or an infection, cause them.

Undernutrition is a very common underlying cause of child mortality. Even children with mild and moderate malnutrition have an increased risk of death. A sick child can be malnourished without you or the family noticing, and may have no complaints that point to malnutrition or anaemia. Module 6 covers this.

cards.front: Then: immunizations, HIV and other problems
cards.back: Modules 7, 8, 9 and additional modules explain these assessments.

read.text: When is urgent referral required?

Children with general danger signs and/or any condition with a red classification require urgent pre-referral treatment and referral. These classifications indicate very serious illness. Look at the CLASSIFY table for general danger signs below: this is a red classification, and the treatments are in the TREAT column on the right.

sections.title: How to refer a child urgently

read.text: Refer a child in four steps, and say what you do when referral is not possible.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: How do you urgently refer the child?
There are four steps to referring a child or a sick young infant to hospital.

steps.title: EXPLAIN the need for referral, and get her agreement
steps.text:
If you suspect that she does not want to take the child, find out why. Possible reasons:
  • She thinks hospitals are places where people often die, and fears her child will die there too.
  • She does not think that the hospital will help the child.
  • She cannot leave home and stay in the hospital: there is no one to take care of her other children, she is needed for farming, or she may lose a job.
  • She does not have money for transport, hospital bills, medicines, or food for herself during the stay.

steps.title: CALM her fears and help her resolve any problems
steps.text:
If she fears her child will die at the hospital, reassure her that the hospital has physicians, supplies, and equipment that can help cure her child.
  • Explain what will happen at the hospital and how that will help her child.
  • If she needs help at home while she is away, ask questions and make suggestions about who could help: for example, whether her husband, sister or another caregiver could help with the other children or with meals.
  • Discuss how she can travel to the hospital. Help arrange transport if necessary.
  • You may not be able to solve her problems and be sure that she goes, but it is important to do everything you can to help.

steps.title: WRITE A REFERRAL NOTE for her to carry
steps.text:
Tell her to give it to the health worker at the hospital. The note should include:
  • The name and age of the infant or child
  • The date and time of referral
  • Description of the child's problems
  • The reason for referral (signs and symptoms for the classification)
  • Treatment that you have given
  • Any other information the hospital needs to care for the child, such as earlier treatment of the illness or immunizations needed
  • Your name and the name of your clinic

steps.title: GIVE SUPPLIES AND INSTRUCTIONS for the way
steps.text:
If the hospital is far, give additional doses of antibiotic and tell her when to give them during the trip (by the dosage schedule on the TREAT chart). If you think she will not actually go to the hospital, give the full course of antibiotics and teach her how to give them.
  • Tell her how to keep the young child warm during the trip.
  • Advise her to continue breastfeeding.
  • If the child has some or severe dehydration and can drink, give her ORS solution for the child to sip frequently on the way.

read.text: Any child with a general danger sign or a serious classification requires urgent referral.
read.label: Remember

read.text: What if referral is not possible?

The best possible treatment for a child with a very severe illness is usually at a hospital. Sometimes referral is not possible or not advisable: the hospital may be too far, may not have adequate equipment or staff, or transport may not be available. Sometimes parents refuse to take a child to a hospital, in spite of the health worker's effort to explain the need for it.

If referral is not possible, do whatever you can to help the family care for the child. Continue pre-referral treatment until the child is able to leave for the hospital. If the child improves on pre-referral treatment, start treatment in the clinic (for example, the YELLOW classification). Advise the caregiver on all available treatment.

To help reduce deaths in severely ill children who cannot be referred, you may need to arrange for the child to stay in or near the clinic, where he may be seen several times a day. If not possible, arrange visits at home. There is more about this in the ANNEX.

read.text: What does the IMNCI process look like for the sick young infant?
IMNCI for the sick young infant follows the same major steps as for the sick child. However, the young infant has some different signs and symptoms to assess, and some treatments are age-appropriate.

sections.title: Introduction to the sick young infant

read.text: Explain why young infants are special and what special care they need.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Why young infants are special
read.caption: Watch this first. It introduces the young infant and the care that protects them.

read.text: A young infant is a child up to 2 months of age. If 2 months old or above, she or he is considered a sick child.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Why are young infants special?
Young infants differ from older infants and children in the ways they show signs of infection. Turn each card.

read.title: Four ways young infants are different

cards.front: They become ill and die very quickly
cards.back: Young infants become ill and die very quickly from serious bacterial infections. Severe infections are the most common serious illness during the first 2 months of life.

cards.front: Low birth weight is a special risk
cards.back: Infants under 2.5 kg at birth are low weight. Infections are particularly dangerous in low birth weight infants. The low weight is due either to poor growth in the womb or to prematurity (being born early).
Infants often show only general signs when seriously ill, such as difficulty in feeding, reduced movements, fever or low body temperature.

Newborn infants are often sick from conditions related to labour and delivery: birth asphyxia, birth trauma, preterm birth (before 37 weeks of pregnancy, with trouble breathing due to immature lungs) and early-onset infections such as sepsis from premature ruptured membranes. These newborns require immediate attention.

read.text: Young infants can become sick and die very quickly.
read.label: Remember

read.text: What are young infants' special care requirements?

Young infants have important care requirements to protect them from infection during the first months of life:

  • Exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding, which gives young infants the nutrients and antibodies they need for healthy growth, development and immune function
  • Keeping infants warm, particularly through skin-to-skin contact
  • Good hygiene: washing hands every time before holding an infant, and keeping the umbilical cord area clean, which is vulnerable to infection
  • Immunizing a young infant on schedule
  • Seeking care immediately if there are signs of severe disease
The IMNCI process (ASSESS, CLASSIFY, TREAT) is the same for young infants and children. However, as infants have some special care requirements, they are assessed for specific symptoms and signs.
Is this important care for a young infant? Sort each card.

items.text: Skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care) to keep the infant warm
Give water regularly to keep the infant hydrated
items.why: Exclusive breastfeeding: breast milk only, no water.

items.text: Seek care immediately if the infant develops signs of serious illness
Change gowns before holding the young infant
items.why: What matters is washing hands before holding the infant.

items.text: Exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding
Give all immunizations at birth, and never again
Give immunizations on schedule
Wash hands before handling the young infant
Rub the young infant with oils, lotion or vaseline to keep the skin moist

read.explanation: Important care: exclusive breastfeeding, keep warm, keep the cord clean, wash hands before holding, immunize on schedule, seek care immediately for signs of serious illness.

NO signs present

sections.title: Assess for severe disease and local infection

read.text: Assess a young infant for very severe disease and local bacterial infection, one sign at a time.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: What is fast breathing in a young infant under 2 months?
feedback: That is for children 12 months up to 5 years.
That is for children 2 up to 12 months.
Right. 60 or more, on a repeat count.

read.text: How will you assess?
You ask the caregiver questions and also make your own observations, following the ASSESS chart. Assess the signs in the order on the chart. The young infant should be calm.

read.caption: Chart booklet: very severe disease and local bacterial infection (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.text: For the first two signs (fast breathing and severe chest indrawing) the young infant must be calm, and may be asleep. If the infant is awake, observe his or her movements. Then pick up the infant, undress him, look at the skin all over his body and measure his temperature. By this time he will probably be awake, so you can observe his movements.

read.title: Assessing for severe disease and local infection, one sign at a time

steps.title: ASK: is your baby having difficulty in feeding?
steps.text: Any difficulty the caregiver mentions is important. An infant who was feeding well earlier but is not feeding well now may have a serious infection. A newborn who has not been able to feed since birth may be premature or have complications such as birth asphyxia. Infants who are not able to feed or are not feeding well should be referred urgently to hospital. Other difficulties (feeding too often or not often enough, not enough milk, sore, flat or inverted nipples) are assessed later during the breastfeeding assessment.

steps.title: ASK: has your baby had convulsions (fits)?
steps.text: Use words the caregiver understands, such as "fits" or "spasms". During a convulsion the arms and legs may become stiff, the infant may stop breathing and become blue. Often there are only rhythmic movements of a part of the body, such as twitching of the mouth or blinking of the eyes. The infant may lose consciousness.

steps.title: LOOK: does the infant have fast breathing?
steps.text: Young infants usually breathe faster than older children: a healthy young infant commonly breathes more than 50 times a minute. So 60 breaths per minute or more is the cut-off. If the first count is 60 or more, repeat the count, because the breathing of a young infant is often irregular (it may stop for a few seconds, then be faster). If the second count is also 60 or more, the infant has fast breathing.

steps.title: LOOK: does the infant have severe chest indrawing?
steps.text: Chest indrawing: the lower chest wall goes IN when the infant breathes IN. Only severe chest indrawing is a serious sign in a young infant: mild chest indrawing is normal because the chest wall is soft. Severe chest indrawing is very deep and easy to see, and is a sign of pneumonia. It must be visible and present all the time you observe the infant.

steps.title: MEASURE the temperature (or feel the infant): fever or low body temperature?
steps.text: Thresholds are for axillary (armpit) temperature; rectal thresholds are about 0.5 °C higher. Without a thermometer, feel the abdomen or armpit. Fever is 37.5 °C or above: uncommon in the first two months, it may mean very severe disease and may be the only sign of a serious bacterial infection. Low body temperature is below 35.5 °C (hypothermia): young infants can respond to infection by dropping their temperature.

steps.title: LOOK at the umbilicus: is it red or draining pus?
steps.text: The cord usually separates one to two weeks after birth and the wound heals within 15 days. Redness of the end of the umbilicus, or pus draining from it, is a sign of umbilical infection. Recognizing and treating it early is essential to prevent sepsis.

steps.title: LOOK for skin pustules
steps.text: Red spots or blisters that contain pus. Examine the skin on the entire body. Are there a few pustules, or many? A severe pustule is large or has redness extending beyond the pustule. Many or severe pustules indicate a serious infection.

steps.title: LOOK at the young infant's movements
steps.text: Young infants often sleep most of the time; this is not a sign of illness. An awake young infant will normally move his arms or legs or turn his head several times a minute. If the infant is awake but has no spontaneous movements, gently stimulate him. If he moves only when stimulated and then stops, or does not move at all, it is a sign of severe disease. An infant who cannot be woken up even after stimulation also has this sign.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: The local bacterial infection row also lists pus draining from the eye. WHO module (page 19): lists only a red or draining umbilicus and skin pustules.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

cards.back: 60 breaths per minute or more, counted twice
37.5 °C or above (axillary)
below 35.5 °C (axillary)
Only SEVERE chest indrawing counts. Mild indrawing is normal in a young infant.

The classification table for severe disease or local bacterial infection has three classifications:

  1. POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red)
  2. LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION (yellow)
  3. SEVERE DISEASE OR LOCAL INFECTION UNLIKELY (green)
Sudan national booklet: The red classification is called "Possible serious bacterial infection or very severe disease". WHO module (page 19): calls it "VERY SEVERE DISEASE".

read.caption: Classify: very severe disease and local bacterial infection

read.title: Very severe disease and local bacterial infection
read.text: Open each card: the signs, then what to do. Pink first, then yellow, then green.

cards.label: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE
cards.signs: Any one of: not feeding well; convulsions; fast breathing (60 breaths per minute or more); severe chest indrawing; fever (37.5 °C or above); low body temperature (less than 35.5 °C); movement only when stimulated or no movement at all.
cards.treat: First dose of IM ampicillin and gentamicin; prevent low blood sugar; keep the infant warm on the way; refer urgently.

cards.label: LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION
cards.signs: Umbilicus red or draining pus; skin pustules; pus draining from the eyes.
cards.treat: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days; teach the mother to treat local infections at home; home care; follow up in 2 days.

cards.label: SEVERE DISEASE OR LOCAL INFECTION UNLIKELY
cards.signs: No signs of very severe disease or local bacterial infection.
cards.treat: Advise the mother on home care for the young infant.

read.text: When you find signs from different rows, always classify with the more severe classification. Signs from RED and YELLOW: classify RED. Signs from YELLOW and GREEN: classify YELLOW. The colour tells you where care is given: RED = refer urgently, YELLOW = treat in the clinic, GREEN = home treatment.
read.label: Several rows?

read.title: The three classifications and your actions

cards.front: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red)
cards.back: One sign is enough. The infant may have a serious disease and be at high risk of death: complications of preterm birth (very low birth weight or birth asphyxia) or a serious infection such as pneumonia, sepsis or meningitis. You do not need to tell these apart to decide the first management. Give the first dose of intramuscular antibiotics, treat to prevent low blood sugar (breast milk, or sugar water if breast milk is not possible; by nasogastric tube if the infant cannot feed), advise the mother to keep the infant warm (low temperature alone can kill young infants) and refer URGENTLY. Malaria is unusual at this age, so no treatment for severe malaria is needed.

Typically an infected umbilicus or a skin infection. Give an appropriate oral antibiotic at home for 5 days, teach the caregiver to treat the local infection at home, advise home care, and follow up in 2 days: bacterial infections can progress rapidly in young infants.

cards.front: SEVERE DISEASE OR LOCAL INFECTION UNLIKELY (green)
cards.back: None of the signs above. Advise the caregiver to give home care.

Stop the assessment and refer straight away

sections.title: Jaundice: what it is and how to assess it

read.text: Tell mild jaundice from jaundice that is a sign of a severe problem, and assess a young infant for jaundice.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: Where do you look to decide if jaundice is severe?
feedback: Right. Yellow palms and soles at any age is severe jaundice.
Look at the palms and soles too.
Look at the skin, palms and soles.

read.title: Jaundice in the young infant
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: After checking for signs of severe disease, you assess the main symptoms. The first is jaundice. LOOK: is the infant jaundiced? If yes, classify using the jaundice table. Then continue the assessment.
What is jaundice?

Jaundice is a yellow discoloration of the skin in young infants. Many normal babies have jaundice during the first week of life, commonly small babies under 2.5 kg at birth or born before 37 weeks. It usually appears on the third or fourth day of life, because the infant's liver is not mature enough to eliminate the bilirubin formed in the body. This jaundice is mild, disappears before 2 weeks of age in full-term babies and by 3 weeks in preterm babies, and needs no treatment.
When is jaundice a sign of a severe problem?

Jaundice that appears on the first day of life is always due to an underlying disease. Deep jaundice that extends to the palms and soles can be severe and needs urgent treatment. Jaundice that persists beyond 2 weeks of age needs further investigation: untreated, it may damage the infant's brain.
Jaundice needs special attention when it appears within 24 hours of birth, reaches the palms and soles, or remains beyond 2 weeks of age.
read.label: Key point

read.text: How will you assess for jaundice?

steps.title: LOOK for yellow skin
steps.text: Look in natural light. Press the skin over the forehead with your fingers to blanch it, remove your fingers and look for yellow discoloration. If there is yellow discoloration, the infant has jaundice.

steps.title: LOOK at the palms and soles
steps.text: Repeat the same on the palms and the soles of the feet. Yellow discoloration here shows severe disease.

steps.title: ASK: when did the jaundice first appear?
steps.text: The timing of the jaundice, and the infant's age, are very important for the classification.

read.text: Check yourself
A baby's skin turns yellow on the first day of life. What does this tell you?
options: It is the mild jaundice that many normal babies have
It is always due to an underlying disease
It matters only if it is still there after 2 weeks
read.explanation: Jaundice that appears on the first day of life is always due to an underlying disease. The mild jaundice of normal babies usually appears on the third or fourth day of life.

read.text: How do you look for jaundice?
options: Ask the caregiver whether the infant looks yellow to her
Look at the infant's face only, in any light
In natural light, press the skin over the forehead to blanch it and look for yellow; then do the same on the palms and soles
read.explanation: Look in natural light. Press the skin over the forehead with your fingers to blanch it, remove your fingers and look for yellow discoloration. Repeat on the palms and the soles of the feet.

cards.signs: Any jaundice if age less than 24 hours; or yellow palms and soles at any age; or any jaundice in an infant weighing less than 2.5 kg.
cards.treat: Prevent low blood sugar; keep the infant warm; refer urgently.

cards.label: JAUNDICE
cards.signs: Jaundice appearing after 24 hours of age, and palms and soles not yellow.
cards.treat: If 14 days or older, refer for assessment; home care; return immediately if palms and soles appear yellow; follow up in 1 day.

cards.label: NO JAUNDICE
cards.treat: Advise the mother on home care for the young infant.

Jaundice that appeared after 24 hours of age, and palms and soles not yellow. Advise home care, advise to return immediately if the palms and soles become yellow, follow up in 1 day. If the infant is 14 days or older, refer for assessment.

sections.title: Diarrhoea in the young infant

read.text: Say when a young infant has diarrhoea, and classify dehydration in a young infant.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: You will learn to assess and classify diarrhoea in Module 4. The process is similar to the sick child. You can look at it now so that you are familiar with the signs when you assess young infants in your clinic.

A young infant has diarrhoea if the stools have changed from the usual pattern and are many and watery (more water than faecal matter). The normally frequent or semi-solid stools of a breastfed baby are not diarrhoea.
read.label: What is diarrhoea in a young infant?

read.caption: Chart booklet: diarrhoea in the young infant (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.title: Classifying dehydration in the young infant

cards.back: Two of: movement only when stimulated or no movement at all; sunken eyes; skin pinch goes back very slowly. With no other severe classification, give fluid for severe dehydration (Plan C). With another severe classification, refer URGENTLY with the mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way and continuing breastfeeding.

Two of: restless and irritable; sunken eyes; skin pinch goes back slowly. Give fluid and breast milk for some dehydration (Plan B). With a severe classification, refer URGENTLY with sips of ORS on the way. Follow up in 2 days if not improving.

Not enough signs to classify as some or severe dehydration. Give fluids to treat diarrhoea at home and continue breastfeeding (Plan A). Advise when to return immediately; follow up in 2 days if not improving.

sections.title: Before referral: what the infant needs

read.text: Say which classifications need urgent referral, what the infant needs before leaving, and how to prevent low blood sugar.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Pre-referral treatment for the young infant
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: Which classifications need urgent referral?

A young infant with any severe (RED) classification needs urgent referral:

  • POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE
  • SEVERE JAUNDICE
  • SEVERE DEHYDRATION in some cases: the infant needs IV fluids. If you can give IV therapy you can treat in the clinic. If you cannot, refer urgently. If the infant has SEVERE DEHYDRATION and another severe classification, refer.
What does the young infant need before referral?

Give all appropriate pre-referral treatments; urgent pre-referral treatments are in bold on the chart. Do not give treatments that are not urgent and would delay referral: for example, do not teach the caregiver to treat a local infection, and do not immunize before referral.
Pre-referral treatment: which classification needs it?
groups: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE

items.text: First dose of intramuscular ampicillin and gentamicin
Treat to prevent low blood sugar
Advise the mother how to keep the infant warm on the way

read.explanation: Severe jaundice gets all the pre-referral treatments of very severe disease except the intramuscular antibiotics. If the infant needs an oral antibiotic for a local bacterial infection and has not had intramuscular antibiotics, give the first oral dose before referral. With severe dehydration and another severe classification, teach the caregiver to give frequent sips of ORS on the way and to continue breastfeeding.

read.text: How will you treat to prevent low blood sugar?

read.title: Prevent low blood sugar: it depends on whether the infant can feed and swallow

steps.title: Able to breastfeed
steps.text: Ask the caregiver to breastfeed.

steps.title: Unable to breastfeed but able to swallow
steps.text: Give 20–50 ml (10 ml/kg) expressed breast milk before departure. If not possible, give 20–50 ml (10 ml/kg) sugar water: dissolve 4 level teaspoons of sugar (20 g) in a 200 ml cup of clean water.

steps.title: Unable to swallow
steps.text: Give 20–50 ml (10 ml/kg) expressed breast milk or sugar water by nasogastric tube.

sections.title: First dose of antibiotics, warmth and referral

read.text: Give the first dose of intramuscular antibiotics, keep the infant warm, and refer the young infant.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: How will you give the first dose of intramuscular antibiotics?

Young infants get two intramuscular antibiotics, gentamicin and ampicillin. Young infants with very severe disease are often infected with a broader range of bacteria than older infants, and the combination is effective against this broader range.

read.caption: The red row with its live doses: open the whole booklet for the dose tables

read.text:
Ampicillin (50 mg/kg): to a 250 mg vial add 2.1 ml sterile water = 250 mg/2.5 ml. Choose the dose from the row closest to the infant's weight.

Gentamicin: read the vial to find its strength and whether to dilute it. When ready to use, the strength should be 10 mg/ml (for example, 80 mg/2 ml vial + 6 ml sterile water). Choose the dose from the row closest to the infant's age and weight: under 7 days 0.5 ml/kg, 7 days or older 0.75 ml/kg.

WeightAmpicillinGentamicin, under 7 daysGentamicin, 7 days or older
Under 1.5 kg0.5 ml0.5 ml0.8 ml
1.5–2.49 kg1.0 ml1.0 ml1.5 ml
2.5–3.49 kg1.5 ml1.5 ml2.25 ml
3.5–4.49 kg2.0 ml2.0 ml3.0 ml
4.5–6 kg2.5 ml2.5 ml3.75 ml

If you have a vial with a different amount, or use a different amount of sterile water, the table is not correct: follow the manufacturer's directions and recalculate the dose. Avoid undiluted 40 mg/ml gentamicin.

Sudan national booklet: Ampicillin 250 mg + 2.1 ml water = 250 mg/2.5 ml, and the doses in the table above (for example 1.5 ml ampicillin for 2.5–3.49 kg). WHO module (page 32): ampicillin 250 mg + 1.3 ml water = 250 mg/1.5 ml, with doses by half-kilogram (1.0 ml for 3–3.5 kg); gentamicin 1.6 ml (under 7 days) or 2.4 ml (7 days or older) for 3–3.5 kg.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Referral is the best option. If referral is not possible, continue ampicillin and gentamicin for at least 5 days: ampicillin twice daily under one week of age and three times daily from one week; gentamicin once daily. See "Where referral is not possible" in the chart booklet annex.
read.label: If the infant cannot go to hospital

read.text: How will you keep the infant warm?

Keeping the infant warm is very important during travel to the hospital. Advise skin-to-skin contact, or keep the infant covered as much as possible at all times: extra clothing (hat, gloves, socks), wrapped in a soft dry cloth and covered with a blanket.
Then refer the young infant

steps.title: Referral note
steps.text: Prepare a referral note and explain to the caregiver why you are referring the infant.

steps.title: Teach care on the way
steps.text: Keeping the infant warm, breastfeeding, giving sips of ORS.

steps.title: Explain why it matters
steps.text: Young infants are particularly vulnerable: when seriously ill they need hospital care promptly. Many cultures have reasons not to take a young infant to hospital; address these reasons and explain that the illness is best treated at the hospital.

sections.title: Treatment in the clinic: oral antibiotic and jaundice

read.text: Decide the treatments for yellow and green classifications, give an oral antibiotic for local bacterial infection, and manage jaundice.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Yellow and green classifications do not need referral. They are treated in the clinic or at home, following the TREAT charts of the young infant section of the chart booklet.

steps.title: Record
steps.text: As you assess and classify, record the treatments for each classification on the recording form.

steps.title: Integrate
steps.text: After the assessment, decide the integrated treatment.

steps.title: Treat
steps.text: Give the necessary treatments in the clinic.

steps.title: Advise
steps.text: Advise the caregiver on home treatment and when to return to the clinic.

read.text: Oral antibiotic for local bacterial infection
Use the chart booklet to find the recommended antibiotic, then the dose for the infant's weight.

Amoxicillin, twice daily for 5 days:

  • Under 4 kg: 2.5 ml syrup (125 mg/5 ml) or ¼ tablet (250 mg)
  • 4 to under 6 kg: 5 ml syrup (125 mg/5 ml) or ½ tablet (250 mg)

Sudan national booklet: Amoxicillin is the oral antibiotic for local bacterial infection. WHO module (page 36): also gives co-trimoxazole as an option (avoid it under 1 month if premature or jaundiced).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Give the first dose in the clinic. Then teach the caregiver how to continue at home: how to measure a dose, how to crush a tablet and mix it with breast milk, and the schedule. Guide her as she gives the first dose, watch her, and ask checking questions.
Managing jaundice

Young infants with JAUNDICE need home care just like those without any problem. They need no medication. Counsel the caregiver to return immediately if the palms and soles become yellow, and follow up in 1 day to see whether the jaundice is worsening. If the infant is 14 days or older, refer to hospital for assessment.

sections.title: Local infections the caregiver can treat at home

read.text: Teach the caregiver to treat skin pustules, umbilical infection and thrush at home.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Local infections the caregiver can treat at home
Three local infections can be treated at home: a red or draining umbilicus, skin pustules, and oral thrush. The caregiver cleans the infected area and applies gentian violet.

read.title: Treat skin pustules or umbilical infection at home (twice daily for 5 days)

steps.title: Gently wash off pus and crusts with soap and water

cards.back: Full-strength (0.5%) gentian violet, twice daily for 5 days.
Half-strength (0.25%) gentian violet, 4 times daily for 7 days.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Thrush: half-strength gentian violet 4 times daily for 7 days. WHO module (page 37): twice daily, stopping after 5 days.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Explain and demonstrate the treatment, then watch and guide the caregiver while she does it. Send supplies home with her. She should return in 2 days, or sooner if the infection worsens. Ask checking questions to be sure she knows how often to treat and when to return.
Practise

sections.title: Provide follow-up care for the sick young infant

read.text: Give follow-up care for local bacterial infection, jaundice and thrush.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Follow-up visits are especially important for young infants because their illness progresses quickly. At a follow-up visit you do two things: reassess the conditions you classified and treated (improving, the same, or worse?), and reassess with IMNCI for any new problems, using a new recording form.

read.title: When to come back for follow-up

cards.back: Jaundice
Local bacterial infection, thrush, feeding problem, diarrhoea (if not improving)
Low weight for age

read.text: The chart booklet has a follow-up box for each condition, after the treatment charts. Each one reassesses by asking, looking, feeling and listening.
Local bacterial infection (follow-up in 2 days)
LOOK at the umbilicus: is it red or draining pus? LOOK at the skin pustules: are there fewer? Are they drying up?
What do you do at the follow-up?

items.text: Less pus and less redness of the umbilicus
items.why: Complete the 5 days of antibiotic, and continue cleaning and gentian violet for 5 days, even though the infant is improving.

items.text: Fewer pustules, drying up
Pustules the same as before
Umbilicus redness worse

read.text: Jaundice (follow-up in 1 day)
LOOK for jaundice: are the palms and soles yellow?

cards.back: Reassure the caregiver and continue home care. Return for follow-up at 2 weeks of age. If jaundice continues beyond 2 weeks of age, refer for further assessment.

cards.front: Not decreased, palms and soles not yellow
cards.back: Advise home care and follow up again in 1 day.
The infant is getting worse: refer urgently to hospital.

read.text: Thrush (follow-up in 2 days)
LOOK for ulcers or white patches in the mouth, and reassess feeding.

cards.front: Better or the same, feeding well
cards.back: Continue half-strength gentian violet for the full course.

cards.front: Worse, or problems attaching or suckling
cards.back: Refer to hospital. The infant must be treated so that he can feed well again as soon as possible.

read.text: What happened to Mimi?

stages.text: Biya took Mimi to the district hospital, where she was admitted to the newborn care ward. She was given intravenous fluids and antibiotics and kept in a warm room. After some time she started to suck well and her temperature returned to 37.0 °C. She was discharged after 5 days.
Two days later Biya brings Mimi to the clinic for her follow-up appointment.
stages.question: What do you do at this visit?
options: Reassess Mimi's conditions and assess her with IMNCI for any new problems
Nothing: the hospital has treated her
stages.explanation: Reassess what was found and treated, and use a new recording form to look for new problems. Counsel Biya on feeding and care.

sections.title: Feeding problems and feeding recommendations

read.text: Explain why some young infants have feeding problems, and give the feeding recommendations for young infants.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Part II of the module is about feeding. Adequate feeding is essential for the infant's health, growth and development. Poor feeding increases the risk of infection and death, impairs growth, and can have lifelong effects such as poor development or obesity.
Assess feeding in every young infant except those with a severe classification: they are referred urgently.
read.label: Key point

read.title: Assessing feeding and breastfeeding
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: Why do some young infants have feeding problems?

Some feeding and weight problems come from prematurity (born before 37 weeks) or low birth weight. A low birth weight baby is more likely to have breathing and feeding problems, to develop infection and to die; those who survive are more likely to have medical and developmental problems. Some communities believe these babies are born to die: you have an important role in changing this belief and helping families give the extra care these babies need.

cards.back: Under 2500 g (2.5 kg)
Under 1500 g (1.5 kg)

read.text: Feeding recommendations for young infants

read.title: All infants up to 6 months should breastfeed

cards.back: Only breast milk: no other food, water or fluids (medicines and vitamins are exceptions). This reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia and death.
As often as the infant wants, day and night.

read.text: If an infant under 6 months is getting other food or fluids, help the caregiver gradually change back to more or exclusive breastfeeding: more frequent, longer breastfeeds, day and night, while gradually reducing other milk or food. Ask her to return for follow-up in 5 days, as she will need support. A mother who is HIV positive needs separate advice (Module 8).
Check yourself
Which birth weight is low birth weight?
read.explanation: Low birth weight is under 2500 g (2.5 kg). Very low birth weight is under 1500 g (1.5 kg).

read.text: What does exclusive breastfeeding mean?
options: Breast milk and a little water in hot weather
Breast milk in the day and other milk at night
Only breast milk: no other food, water or fluids
read.explanation: Exclusively means only breast milk: no other food, water or fluids (medicines and vitamins are exceptions). All infants up to 6 months should breastfeed exclusively, on demand, at least 8 times in 24 hours.

sections.title: Part A: assess for a feeding problem or low weight

read.text: Ask the Part A questions, determine weight for age and look for thrush.
read.label: In this lesson
Before you start
read.text: How many breastfeeds in 24 hours does a young infant need?
feedback: Fewer than 8 is a feeding problem.
Right.
8 or more is enough.

read.text: Part A: assess for feeding problem or low weight

read.caption: Chart booklet: feeding problem or low weight (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.title: Part A, one question at a time

steps.title: ASK: is there any difficulty feeding?
steps.text: Any difficulty is important: the caregiver may need counselling or specific help. If she says the infant is not able to feed, watch a breastfeed or a cup feed to see what she means. An infant who is not able to feed may have a serious infection and should be referred urgently.

steps.title: ASK: is the infant breastfed? How many times in 24 hours?
steps.text: The recommendation is 8 or more times in 24 hours, as often and for as long as the infant wants, day and night.

steps.title: ASK: does the infant receive other foods or drinks? How often?
steps.text: Other milk, juice, tea, thin porridge, dilute cereal or even water. Ask how often and how much: is the infant mostly breastfed, or mostly fed on other foods? What is used to feed the infant?

steps.title: DETERMINE weight for age
steps.text: Use the weight-for-age chart in the chart booklet, the one for boys or the one for girls (birth to 6 months): find where the lines for weight and age meet. Ages are in weeks up to 13 weeks, then in months. Below the -2 line is low weight for age.

steps.title: LOOK for ulcers or white patches in the mouth (thrush)
steps.text: Look at the tongue and inside the cheek. Thrush looks like milk curds on the cheek or a thick white coating of the tongue. Try to wipe it off: the white patches of thrush remain.

read.text: A young infant is 6 weeks old and weighs 3 kg. The point where the lines for 6 weeks and 3 kg meet is BELOW the -2 line: the infant is low weight for age.
read.label: Worked example

read.title: Plot the worked example yourself
read.text: Plot this young infant on the girls' weight-for-age chart from the chart booklet. Find 6 weeks along the bottom and 3 kg up the side, and tap where they meet.
read.explanation: At 6 weeks the -2 line on the girls' chart is close to 3.5 kg, so 3 kg is below it: low weight for age.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: the September 2023 edition has separate weight-for-age charts for boys and for girls from birth to 6 months, drawn as WHO z-score lines (-3, -2, 0, +2, +3). Low weight for age is below the -2 line. WHO module (page 46): uses one young infant chart for boys and girls, with a line marked "low weight for age" (and a "very low" line used only for older children).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

sections.title: Part B: assess breastfeeding

read.text: Watch a breastfeed and judge attachment and suckling.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Part B: assess breastfeeding

Assess breastfeeding if the infant has no indication for urgent referral and:

  • is feeding less than 8 times in 24 hours, or
  • is taking other food or drinks (mixed feeding), or
  • the caregiver's answers show a difficulty with breastfeeding, or
  • is low weight for age (often due to low birth weight; these infants are likely to have breastfeeding problems)

read.caption: The breastfeeding assessment on the recording form

read.title: Part B, one step at a time

steps.title: ASK: has the infant breastfed in the previous hour?
steps.text: If yes, ask the caregiver to tell you when the infant is willing to feed again; meanwhile check immunizations or start a treatment (such as an antibiotic for local infection, or ORS). If not, ask her to put the infant to the breast and observe a whole feed if possible, or at least 4 minutes. Sit quietly and watch.

steps.title: LOOK: is the infant able to attach?
steps.text: Look for the four signs of good attachment. Is the infant well attached, not well attached, or not attaching at all?

steps.title: LOOK: is the infant suckling effectively?
steps.text: Slow deep sucks, sometimes pausing. Clear a blocked nose if it interferes with breastfeeding.

cards.back: 1. Chin touching the breast (or very close). 2. Mouth wide open. 3. Lower lip turned outward. 4. More areola visible above than below the mouth.

cards.front: Not well attached: any of these
cards.back: 1. Chin not touching the breast. 2. Mouth not wide open, lips pushed forward. 3. Lower lip turned in. 4. More areola (or an equal amount) visible below the mouth than above it.
A very sick infant who cannot take the nipple into his mouth and keep it there to suck. He is not able to breastfeed at all.

read.text: Poor attachment can cause pain and damage to the nipples, or the infant may not remove breast milk well, causing engorgement. The infant may be unsatisfied and want to feed very often or for a very long time, may get too little milk and not gain weight, or the milk may dry up. All these problems may improve if attachment improves.
Exercise H: good or poor attachment? Sort each sign.

items.text: Chin away from breast
More areola visible above than below the mouth
Narrow mouth with lips pushed forward
Equal amount of areola visible below and above the mouth
Mouth wide open
Lower lip turned outward
Chin touching breast
Lower lip turned in

cards.back: Slow deep sucks, sometimes pausing. You may see or hear swallowing. At the end the infant releases the breast on his own, looks relaxed, sleepy and loses interest in the breast.
Only rapid, shallow sucks; you may see the cheeks drawing in. No swallowing seen or heard. Not satisfied at the end: restless, cries, tries to suckle again or keeps breastfeeding for a long time.
Not able to suck breast milk into his mouth and swallow: not able to breastfeed at all.

steps.title: Good attachment
steps.text: Chin touching breast, mouth wide open, lower lip turned outward, more areola above than below.

steps.title: Not well attached
steps.text: Compare: chin not touching, mouth not wide open, areola equal above and below.

steps.title: Good positioning
steps.text: Head and body straight, facing the breast, close to the mother, whole body supported.

read.note: Exercise I: match each infant with how well they are suckling.

read.title: Demonstration: breastfeeding assessment
read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 2. All the steps of the breastfeeding assessment, with examples of good attachment and suckling.

sections.title: Classify feeding problems and low weight

read.text: Classify feeding, classify Mimi, and say what to do when an infant takes no breast milk at all.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: How will you classify feeding problems and low weight?

cards.back: Not well attached, or not suckling effectively, or less than 8 breastfeeds in 24 hours, or receives other foods or drinks, or low weight for age, or thrush. Advise breastfeeding as often and as long as the infant wants, day and night (short feeds are an important reason for not getting enough milk), and teach the specific help needed: positioning and attachment, treating thrush. Follow up a feeding problem or thrush in 2 days, low weight in 14 days.

Exclusively and frequently breastfed, and not low weight for age (not below the -2 line). Advise home care and praise the mother. She may still need counselling to make sure the infant gains weight well.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: The yellow row lists: teach positioning and attachment; increase breastfeeds; reduce other foods or drinks and use a cup; refer for breastfeeding counselling and possible relactation if not breastfeeding; treat thrush; keep the infant warm; follow-up. WHO module (page 51): also lists "if not able to attach well immediately, teach the mother to express breast milk and feed by a cup" and "advise about correctly preparing breast-milk substitutes and using a cup".
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: "Not able to feed" is not on this table because you assessed it with the signs of very severe disease. It is a severe (red) sign: the infant gets the same pre-referral treatment as very severe disease and is referred urgently.
read.label: Why is "not able to feed" missing?

read.text: How did you assess Mimi's feeding?

stages.text: Biya breastfeeds Mimi. Mimi had not been feeding well for a few days, and since this morning she is not taking the breast at all. When Biya tries, Mimi will not attach: a severe sign you already classified. You cannot assess breastfeeding. Mimi has no thrush or ulcers.
Mimi is 6 weeks old and weighs 3.1 kg, less than at birth.
stages.question: Is Mimi low weight for age?
stages.explanation: On the girls' weight-for-age chart her weight falls below the -2 line: low weight for age.

read.text: If the infant takes no breast milk at all

Skip Parts A and B and use the chart for non-breastfed infants: ask what milk is given, how many times, how much, how it is prepared (let the mother show you), whether any breast milk is given, what other foods and fluids, cup or bottle, and how the utensils are cleaned. This chart is also used when an HIV-positive mother has chosen not to breastfeed. Module 8 covers it, with counselling HIV-positive women on infant feeding.

read.title: Feeding problem or low weight
read.text: Open each card: the signs, then what to do. Pink first, then yellow, then green.

cards.label: FEEDING PROBLEM OR LOW WEIGHT
cards.signs: Not well attached; or not suckling effectively; or less than 8 breastfeeds in 24 hours; or receives other foods or drinks; or low weight for age; or thrush.
cards.treat: Teach positioning and attachment; advise to breastfeed more often, day and night; counsel about other foods and a cup; treat thrush; follow up a feeding problem or thrush in 2 days and low weight in 14 days.

cards.label: NO FEEDING PROBLEM
cards.signs: Not low weight for age and no other signs of inadequate feeding.
cards.treat: Advise the mother on home care; praise her for feeding the infant well.

sections.title: Practise: classify feeding problems

read.text: Classify the feeding of three young infants, and practise the questions you ask a mother.
read.label: In this lesson

dialogue.text: How many times does Layla breastfeed in 24 hours, day and night?
Does she get any other food or drink?

stages.question: Is this a feeding problem?
options: Yes: less than 8 times in 24 hours
No: only breast milk is fine
Only if she is losing weight
stages.explanation: A young infant should breastfeed 8 times or more in 24 hours.
feedback: Right.
Exclusive breastfeeding is good, but 6 times is not enough.
Fewer than 8 feeds is a problem whatever the weight.

dialogue.text: She sleeps a lot at night.

stages.question: What do you advise?
options: Breastfeed as often and for as long as she wants, day and night
stages.explanation: Advise the mother to breastfeed as often and for as long as the infant wants, day and night.
feedback: Right.
A young infant needs breast milk only.
Night feeds are important.

read.label: Test your skill
read.title: Classify feeding problem or low weight

cases.text: Layla is breastfed 6 times in 24 hours. She takes no other food or drink. Her weight for age is not low. She is well positioned and well attached and suckles effectively. No thrush.

record.title: Check for feeding problem or low weight

cases.question: How do you classify Layla's feeding?
feedback: Right. Breastfeeding less than 8 times in 24 hours is a feeding problem.
Her attachment is good, but she breastfeeds only 6 times. A young infant should breastfeed 8 times or more in 24 hours.
cases.explanation: Advise the mother to breastfeed as often and for as long as the infant wants, day and night.

cases.text: Yasir breastfeeds 10 times in 24 hours, day and night. He gets no other food or drink. His weight for age is not low. He is well attached and suckles effectively. No thrush.

record.title: Check for feeding problem or low weight

cases.question: How do you classify Yasir's feeding?
feedback: Yasir has no sign of a feeding problem and his weight is not low.
Right. Praise the mother for feeding him well.
cases.explanation: No feeding problem: advise the mother on home care for the young infant and praise her.

cases.text: Rana breastfeeds 9 times in 24 hours. Her mother also gives her water and goat's milk from a bottle. She is well attached.

record.title: Check for feeding problem or low weight
lines: Other foods or drinks: water, goat's milk

cases.question: What is Rana's feeding problem? Select all that apply.
options: She receives other foods or drinks
She is fed from a bottle
feedback: 9 times in 24 hours is enough: 8 or more.
Right. A young infant should have breast milk only.
Right. Counsel the mother to stop the bottle and use a cup if she must give other milk.
cases.explanation: Counsel the mother to breastfeed more, reduce other foods and drinks, and use a cup instead of a bottle.

sections.title: Check immunizations and other problems

read.text: Check a young infant's immunizations, other problems and the mother's health.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Immunizations protect young infants from infections that are especially dangerous at their age. Check whether the infant has had all the immunizations recommended for his age, and whether any are needed today. Counsel caregivers on immunizing on schedule.

read.caption: The immunization row of the national young infant recording form

read.title: The national schedule for young infants

cards.back: OPV 0, BCG
OPV 1, Rota 1, PCV 1, Penta 1, IPV 1
OPV 2, Rota 2, PCV 2, Penta 2

read.text: Sudan national booklet: The schedule above (Penta includes hepatitis B and Hib). WHO module (page 54): lists hepatitis B0 at birth and DPT, Hib and hepatitis B at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, with vitamin A 200 000 IU to the mother within 6 weeks of delivery.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Do not give OPV 0 to an infant more than 14 days old. If an infant has not had OPV 0 by 15 days, wait and give OPV 1 at 6 weeks. Give the vaccines the infant needs today and record the date of the next dose. If the infant is being referred, do not immunize before referral.
read.label: Remember

read.text: Other problems and the mother's health

Assess any other problem the caregiver mentions or that you see. If you think the infant has a serious problem, or you do not know how to help, refer. Ask about the caregiver's own health: it tells you about her, the child's health and the household, and helps you counsel her.

Assessing the caregiver's well-being includes:

  • Preventing and detecting postpartum complications (infections, bleeding, anaemia)
  • Preventing or managing anaemia (iron and folic acid)
  • Information and counselling on nutrition, safe sex and family planning
  • Providing contraception
  • Planning postnatal care, with advice on danger signs and emergency preparedness
  • Promoting use of insecticide-treated nets
Mimi is 6 weeks old and due for her 6-week vaccines, but she is being referred urgently. What do you do?
read.answer: Do not immunize now: it would delay referral. Write the vaccines due on her referral note so the hospital staff can decide. Biya came for her own postnatal check: stabilize Mimi first, then assess Biya's health and note it on the form.

sections.title: Counsel on feeding: positioning and attachment

read.text: Give the most important messages about the young infant, and teach a mother correct positioning and attachment.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Counselling a mother on breastfeeding
read.caption: Watch this first.

read.text: Counselling the caregiver is a vital part of IMNCI for the young infant: families need to understand the care that protects their infant. Review the good communication skills from the introduction.

read.title: The most important messages about the young infant

cards.back: Exclusively and on demand.
Especially low weight infants.
Before handling the infant.
If the infant shows any sign of severe disease or local infection.

read.text: The feeding lessons cover four topics: positioning and attachment, expressing breast milk, feeding by cup, and other feeding problems. The lesson on infant care covers the other care.
Feeding 1: teach correct positioning and attachment

An infant may be poorly attached or not suckle effectively because he was small and weak, breastfeeding started late, he had bottle feeds in the first days, or his mother is inexperienced or had a difficulty such as flat nipples with nobody to help. Make sure the mother is comfortable and relaxed, for example sitting on a low seat with her back straight.

steps.title: Hold: head and body in line
steps.text: Show her how to hold her infant with his head and body in line,

steps.title: Hold: nose opposite the nipple
steps.text: facing the breast, with his nose opposite the nipple,

steps.title: Hold: close to her body
steps.text: held close to her body,

steps.title: Hold: whole body supported
steps.text: with his whole body supported, not just the neck and shoulders.

steps.title: Attach: touch the lips with the nipple
steps.text: Show her how to help the infant attach.

steps.title: Attach: wait for a wide-open mouth
Attach: move the infant quickly onto the breast
steps.text: Aim his lower lip well below the nipple.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: Look for signs of good attachment and effective suckling. If not good, try again.

cards.back: Always watch a breastfeed before helping, so you understand her situation. Do not rush to make her do something different.
Say something encouraging: "She really wants your breast milk, doesn't she?"
"Breastfeeding might be more comfortable if your baby took a larger mouthful of breast. Would you like me to show you how?"
Explain and demonstrate, then let her position and attach the infant herself.
Look again for good attachment and suckling. If not good, ask her to take the infant off and try again.
Once suckling well, she should not stop the feed before the infant wants to.

read.title: Demonstration: teach correct positioning and attachment
read.caption: WHO course DVD, disc 2. Good and poor positioning, and how to show the caregiver how to position.

read.text: Check yourself
A mother's infant is poorly attached. What do you do first?
options: Watch a breastfeed, so that you understand her situation
Take the infant and attach him yourself
Tell her to change the way she holds the infant
read.explanation: Always watch a breastfeed before helping. Do not rush to make her do something different, and do not take over: explain and demonstrate, then let her position and attach the infant herself.

read.text: When the mother helps her infant attach, what does she wait for before moving him onto the breast?
read.explanation: She touches the infant's lips with her nipple, waits for a wide-open mouth, then moves the infant quickly onto the breast, aiming his lower lip well below the nipple.

sections.title: Expressing breast milk and feeding by cup

read.text: Teach a mother to express breast milk and to feed her infant by cup.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Feeding 2: teach the mother to express breast milk

Expressing is usually needed for infants who do not suck well but can swallow, often low birth weight babies. It also relieves engorgement, feeds a sick infant who cannot suckle enough, keeps up the supply when the mother or infant is ill, and leaves milk for the infant when the mother goes out or to work.

cards.back: Hand expression needs no appliance, so she can do it anywhere. It is easier when the breasts are soft: teach it on the first or second day after delivery, not the third when the breasts are full. If her own technique works, let her continue.
Breasts are easily hurt if someone else tries. Show on your own body, a model breast, or the soft part of your arm, while she copies you. If you must touch her, be very gentle.
On the first day, within six hours of delivery if possible: even a few drops of colostrum help milk production begin.
As often as the infant would breastfeed: at least every 3 hours, including at night. Long gaps reduce the milk.
Let her express the second half of each breast into a different container and offer it first: more hind milk gives a low birth weight infant extra energy to grow.

read.title: Teach the mother to express breast milk

steps.title: Prepare a cup
steps.text: A cup, glass or jug with a wide mouth, washed with soap and water. Pour boiling water in, leave a few minutes, then pour it out.

steps.title: Hold the container
steps.text: Under the nipple and areola.

steps.title: Place thumb and finger
steps.text: Thumb on top of the breast, first finger underneath, opposite each other, at least 4 cm from the tip of the nipple.

steps.title: Compress and release
steps.text: Press and release the breast between finger and thumb a few times. If no milk comes, move them a little closer to the nipple and try again.

steps.title: All the way around
steps.text: Compress and release all around the breast, at the same distance from the nipple. Do not squeeze the nipple, rub the skin or slide the fingers.

steps.title: Both breasts
steps.text: Express one breast until the milk just drips, then the other.

steps.title: Alternate
steps.text: 5 or 6 times, for at least 20 to 30 minutes. Stop when the milk drips from the start.

read.text: Feeding 3: teach feeding by cup
An infant who cannot breastfeed should get expressed breast milk by cup. If the mother cannot or has chosen not to breastfeed, give a breast-milk substitute by cup.

steps.title: Protect the clothes
steps.text: Put a cloth on the infant's front, as some milk may spill.

steps.title: Hold the infant semi-upright on the lap
Put a measured amount of milk in the cup
Rest the cup lightly on the lower lip
Tip the cup so the milk just reaches the lips
Let the infant take the milk himself
steps.text: Do NOT pour the milk into the infant's mouth.

read.text: Cup, bottle or spoon? Sort each statement.

items.text: Easy to clean with soap and water if boiling is not possible
Often carried around for a long time, giving bacteria time to breed
Cannot be left beside the infant: whoever feeds must hold and look at him
Needs three hands: the infant, the cup of milk and the spoon
Does not interfere with suckling at the breast, and lets the infant control his intake
Safe if the mother prefers it and gives enough, but slow and hard at night

read.explanation: Feeding from a cup is safer than a bottle. Cups are usually easier than spoons, though spoons are safe; for a very ill infant with difficult breathing a spoon is sometimes easier for a short time.

sections.title: Other feeding problems and follow-up

read.text: Counsel on other feeding problems, and give follow-up care for feeding problems, thrush and low weight for age.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Feeding 4: other feeding problems

cards.back: Increase the frequency: breastfeed as often and as long as the infant wants, day and night.
Breastfeed more, reduce the other foods or drinks and if possible stop them. Give any other drinks by cup, not bottle.
Consider referral for breastfeeding counselling and possible relactation. Advise on choosing and correctly preparing a breast-milk substitute, given by cup, not bottle.

read.text: Follow-up for feeding problems
Young infants come back sooner than older children because they should be growing fast and are at higher risk if they do not gain weight, especially after a change in how they are fed.

read.title: Feeding problem or thrush: follow-up in 2 days

cards.back: Check the chart or follow-up note for the problem found and what you recommended.
How have you carried out the recommendations? Any problems?

On new or continuing problems, using "Counsel the mother about feeding problems" and "Teach correct positioning and attachment". For example, if you advised stopping water by bottle and breastfeeding more, check how often she breastfeeds now and whether she stopped the bottle.

read.title: Low weight for age: follow-up in 14 days

cards.back: Praise the caregiver and encourage her to continue.
Praise her. Weigh again within a month or at the next immunization. Many low birth weight infants stay low weight for age but feed and gain weight well.

cards.front: Still low weight, still a feeding problem
cards.back: Counsel on the problem and see the infant again in 14 days, and every few weeks until feeding and gaining weight well.

cards.front: Lost weight or no gain in 14 days
cards.back: Refer to hospital. Also refer if you think the problem will not improve.

sections.title: Counsel the caregiver on infant care

read.text: Counsel the caregiver on keeping the infant warm, good hygiene and when to come back.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: After feeding, advise the caregiver on three more topics: keeping the infant warm, good hygiene, and when to come back.
Infant care 1: keep the infant warm
Keep the newborn's temperature between 36.5 and 37.4 °C. Low temperature harms the sick newborn and increases the risk of death. Low birth weight infants need more attention to warmth.

• Keep the infant in bed in a warm room, at least 25 °C
  • Avoid bathing a low weight infant
  • Keep the infant dry at all times
  • Feel the hands and feet now and then to make sure they are warm
Skin-to-skin contact is the best way to re-warm an infant with cold hands and feet, and to stop the infant getting cold.
read.label: Key point

read.title: Skin-to-skin contact (the mother or any adult)

steps.title: Undress the infant gently
steps.text: Except for cap, nappy and socks. Give the mother privacy and let her sit or recline comfortably.

steps.title: Place the infant on her bare chest
steps.text: Upright and extended, between her breasts.

steps.title: Turn the head to one side
steps.text: To keep the airway clear.

steps.title: Cover
steps.text: With her blouse or gown, then wrap mother and baby with an extra blanket or shawl.

read.text: If skin-to-skin contact is not possible, dress and wrap the infant with head, hands and feet well covered, hold him close in a warmed room, and breastfeed frequently.
Infant care 2: good hygiene

cards.back: Everyone in the household washes hands before handling the infant and after using the toilet. Demonstrate washing with soap and water: long enough, and scrubbing the nails.

cards.front: Keep the cord clean and dry
cards.back: Until the stump falls off. Rubbing alcohol, if available, helps keep it dry (it is very dangerous to drink: store it safely); otherwise gently clean with clean water and soap. The cord usually separates one to two weeks after birth and heals within 15 days. Never remove the stump, even if it seems about to fall.

read.text: Infant care 3: when to come back
Explain both kinds of visit fully: they are different.

cards.back: To check the conditions you classified today: jaundice in 1 day; local bacterial infection, thrush, feeding problem or diarrhoea in 2 days; low weight for age in 14 days.
If the infant breastfeeds poorly, feels unusually cold, is less active, breathes fast or with difficulty, becomes sicker, develops a fever, or the palms and soles become yellow.

read.text: Teach the caregiver these signs using the mother's card, and ask checking questions to be sure she knows when to come back immediately.

read.text: Use your chart booklet and the young infant recording forms as you practise in the clinic. In the coming days, focus on these skills.

Difficulty feeding, convulsions, breathing rate, severe chest indrawing, temperature, umbilicus, skin pustules, movements.
Jaundice and diarrhoea in every infant.
Pre-referral treatments and referral notes, preventing low blood sugar, antibiotics and care for local infections.
Assess feeding problems and low weight; assess breastfeeding (attachment and suckling); check immunizations, other problems and the caregiver's own health.
Positioning and attachment, expressing breast milk, cup feeding, other feeding problems.
Keeping warm and skin-to-skin care, hygiene and handwashing, follow-up, signs to return immediately.
