exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Pre-test
narrative: Before you begin studying this module, quickly practice your knowledge with the questions below. Do not look up the answers. This is for your own exercise. After you finish the module, you will answer the same questions. This will demonstrate to you what you have learned during the course of the module!

questions.question: If a child arrives at your clinic with a sign of serious illness, they should be immediately referred. What are these signs?
points: Child is lethargic or unconscious
Child is vomiting everything
Child has had convulsions, or is convulsing now
Child cannot breastfeed or drink
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: When is a child lethargic?
options: The child will not wake, even after shaking
The child is sleeping more often than usual, but will wake up if you set them down to walk
The child is drowsy and will not follow movement or noise in the room
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: When is a child unconscious?
options: The child will not wake, even after shaking. However, his eyes might be open.
The child is drowsy and will not follow movement or noise in the room
The child is sleeping very deeply
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: If you identify a child with serious illness that requires referral, your course of action is:
options: Stop your assessment of the child, and tell the caregiver they must hurry to the hospital
Provide urgent treatments, prepare the caregiver for travel to the hospital, and prepare supplies and a referral note
Keep the child at your clinic to monitor them and see if they will improve during the course of the day, and then refer only when necessary
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.3 Care when urgent referral is required.

questions.question: Why do some children require urgent referral?
options: The parents do not want to receive care in the clinic
It is quickest if the child receives important care at a different facility
They show signs of serious illness that require advanced care that is usually available at a referral facility, like a hospital.
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 and 1.3.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Exercise C (Salina, 15 months)
narrative: Salina is 15 months old. She weighs 8.5 kg. Her temperature is 38.5 °C.
The health worker asked, "What are the child's problems?" The mother said, "Salina has been coughing for 4 days, and she is not eating well."
This is Salina's initial visit for this problem.
The health worker checked Salina for general danger signs. He asked, "Is Salina able to drink or breastfeed?" The mother said, "No. Salina does not want to breastfeed."
The health worker gave Salina some water. She was too weak to lift her head. She was not able to drink from a cup.
Next he asked the mother, "Is she vomiting?" The mother said, "No."
Then he asked, "Has she had convulsions?" The mother said, "No."
The health worker looked to see if Salina was lethargic or unconscious. When the health worker and the mother were talking, Salina watched them and looked around the room.
learningPoints: Salina was not able to drink from a cup, so she has the general danger sign "not able to drink or breastfeed".
She watched the health worker and her mother and looked around the room, so she is not lethargic.
One general danger sign is enough: the danger sign is present, and Salina needs urgent referral.
exercises.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 25. Her problems: cough for 4 days, not eating well. Initial visit. Circle NOT ABLE TO DRINK OR BREASTFEED; danger sign present: Yes.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Lebo, 19 months (the module case)
narrative: Lebo's grandmother carries him into the clinic. Lebo does not look well. She has walked for one hour to the clinic. She tells you that she is also taking care of 4 other grandchildren. Lebo is her youngest grandchild and she is very worried about him. She says he is acting very unwell and has had a cough for 7 days.

She tells you this is the first time she is bringing Lebo in to the clinic. You ask her how old Lebo is. She says he is 19 months old. You ask Lebo's grandmother her name. She tells you that her name is Nthabeleng.

What is Lebo's problem? Nthabeleng tells you that Lebo has had a cough for 7 days. She also says that he has not been eating well. Nthabeleng is very worried about this. She says that in the past two days, he cannot take anything at all and she says he is very weak. This is concerning to you.

Is Lebo coming for an initial or follow-up visit? Nthabeleng told you that this is her first time bringing him to the clinic for this issue. This is an initial visit. Lebo's temperature and weight were recorded when he came into the clinic, he weighs 10 kg and his temperature is 37 Celsius.

You ask if Lebo is able to drink or breastfeed, and Nthabeleng says, "no, not today, he is too tired." You try to give him some water from a cup but he is too weak and does not swallow. You ask Nthabeleng if Lebo is vomiting, and she says "no." You ask if Lebo is having convulsions, and Nthabeleng says "no."

You look at Lebo's condition. He is not paying attention to you or Nthabeleng as you talk, and only stares ahead. You snap your fingers in front of his face, but he does not look at the fingers. You ask Nthabeleng to bounce Lebo and speak to him, and when she says "Lebo! Lebo!" he does not look up at her.
learningPoints: Lebo is showing two general danger signs - he is unable to drink and lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.
exercises.explain: Lebo is showing two general danger signs - he is unable to drink and lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Exercise D (true or false)
narrative: What will you do for the children who have general danger signs? Which statements below are true, and which are false?
When you check your answers, the true version of each false statement is shown.

questions.question: Stop immediately and send the child to the hospital
questions.explain: The true statement: Continue the assessment quickly, identify all pre-referral treatments needed, treat, and refer urgently. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: Continue the assessment, determine pre-referral treatment, treat, and refer.
questions.explain: True. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: Continue to assess the child and send child to hospital with referral note about all of the treatments you identified.
questions.explain: The true statement: You should deliver the necessary pre-referral treatment before they leave your clinic for the hospital. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: If referral is not possible, there is nothing you can do. Send the child home.
questions.explain: The true statement: You can provide essential care (further discussed in Annex), work with the family to encourage them to go to the hospital, or bring the child near to the clinic to monitor treatment and progress. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Post-test
narrative: Before you began studying this module, you practiced your knowledge. Now that you have finished the module, answer the same questions and see how much you have learned.

questions.question: If a child arrives at your clinic with a sign of serious illness, they should be immediately referred. What are these signs?
points: Child is lethargic or unconscious
Child is vomiting everything
Child has had convulsions, or is convulsing now
Child cannot breastfeed or drink
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: When is a child lethargic?
options: The child will not wake, even after shaking
The child is sleeping more often than usual, but will wake up if you set them down to walk
The child is drowsy and will not follow movement or noise in the room
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: When is a child unconscious?
options: The child will not wake, even after shaking. However, his eyes might be open.
The child is drowsy and will not follow movement or noise in the room
The child is sleeping very deeply
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 Checking all sick children.

questions.question: If you identify a child with serious illness that requires referral, your course of action is:
options: Stop your assessment of the child, and tell the caregiver they must hurry to the hospital
Provide urgent treatments, prepare the caregiver for travel to the hospital, and prepare supplies and a referral note
Keep the child at your clinic to monitor them and see if they will improve during the course of the day, and then refer only when necessary
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.3 Care when urgent referral is required.

questions.question: Why do some children require urgent referral?
options: The parents do not want to receive care in the clinic
It is quickest if the child receives important care at a different facility
They show signs of serious illness that require advanced care that is usually available at a referral facility, like a hospital.
questions.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 24. Revise: 1.2 and 1.3.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Logbook test
narrative: Below are questions about the module. You are allowed to use your Chart Booklet as you answer these questions. You should not use your study modules.

questions.question: According to IMCI charts, a sick child is:
options: 2 months up to 5 years of age
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: What is the first thing you do when a caregiver and child enter your clinic room?
options: Take the child and examine him
Greet the caregiver to make her feel welcome
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Sami is 2 months old. Sami is a:
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: What important information do you need about the child before you begin your assessment?
options: If the child has general danger signs
Age, weight, temperature, child's problem according to caregiver, and if the visit is initial or follow-up
Why the caregiver came to the clinic
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: What is a general danger sign?
options: A sign that a sick young infant is ill
A sign that the child is beginning to get sick, so the mother should watch him more carefully at home
A sign of very serious illness in a sick child, which requires urgent referral
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Which of the following is a general danger sign in sick children?
options: Unable to breastfeed, eat, or drink
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: How do you check if a child is unable to breastfeed or drink?
options: You can tell by looking because the child will be small
Ask the caregiver to give a drink or clean water or breast milk. See if the child will take the liquid into his mouth and swallow it.
Look at the child's lips to see if they are dry
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: How would you explain "convulsions" to a caregiver?
options: The child's arms and legs stiffen, and he might lose consciousness.
The child will fall on the floor and his body will shake violently.
The child's face muscles will twitch.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: How will you determine if a child is vomiting everything?
options: Ask if the child has been vomiting frequently.
Ask the caregiver if the child has vomited everything that they swallowed or drank. If they are unsure, give the child something to drink and see if they vomit.
Ask if the child has vomited at least 5 times in the past 24 hours, because the frequency of vomiting determines this sign.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child is lethargic, how does he look and act?
options: He is drowsy and is not alert or awake. He will not show interest in what is happening around him, he only stares ahead.
His eyes are closed, and he appears unconscious.
He will respond once you speak or clap.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child is unconscious, how does he look and act?
options: His eyes follow your hand if you wave in front of his face.
He will not wake, even when someone shakes him. His eyes could be closed or open. If they are open, they do not follow any objects.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child has a general danger sign, what are the steps taken?
options: Stop everything and send the child to the hospital.
Complete the IMCI assessment without delay so that you can determine if the child has any other critical health issues. Identify and give pre-referral treatments, and prepare a referral note.
Counsel the mother on home treatment and feeding
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child has a severe (RED) classification and needs to be urgently referred, how do you determine the pre-referral treatment?
options: Use your best guess to decide on a treatment for whatever is causing the severe illness
No pre-referral treatment needed, send the child immediately to the hospital to not delay.
Pre-referral treatments are listed in bold type in the classification tables. Give all pre-referral treatments for all classifications.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Important pre-referral treatments include:
options: Breastfeeding assessments and counselling for feeding problems
Oral rehydration therapy in the clinic
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Every child is checked for general danger signs.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Only children who are unconscious require urgent referral.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: A child whose nose is blocked may have trouble breastfeeding. You must clear the nose to check if the child is able to drink.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child has a general danger sign, stop the assessment immediately and send them to the hospital.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If referral is not possible, there is not much you can do, so you should send the child home.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: IMCI for the sick child and young infant are exactly the same.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Pre-test
narrative: Before you begin studying this module, check what you know. Do not look up the answers. After the module you will answer the same questions.

questions.question: Why do young infants require different care than sick children?
options: Young infants are much quicker to recover from illness because they are young.
Young infants show signs of illness differently. They can also become ill and die from an infection very quickly.
Young infants very rarely get sick.
questions.explain: Introduction to the sick young infant: young infants are special.

questions.question: Which of the following is important care for a young infant?
options: Keeping the infant loosely bundled so he can begin to move his arms and legs
Keeping the umbilical cord moist so that it falls off quickly
Keeping the infant warm through skin-to-skin care
questions.explain: Introduction and infant care lessons: keep the infant warm; the cord is kept clean and dry.

questions.question: What are the feeding recommendations for sick young infants?
options: Exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding for at least 6 months
Breastfeeding and additional sources of fluid, like water, to hydrate
Soft complementary foods as soon as the child is ready
questions.explain: Feeding lessons: exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding. (The printed WHO answer key gives B, which contradicts the module text.)

questions.question: What are signs that a young infant is seriously ill and needs urgent referral and care?
options: Breathing more than 60 breaths per minute
Some jaundice, where the eyes are yellow but not the palms or soles
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease: fast breathing (60 or more, counted twice) is a sign of very severe disease. A few pustules are a local infection.

questions.question: A young infant presents at your clinic. The caregiver says the infant had been feeding well, but in the past 2 days is unable to breastfeed at all. What actions will you take?
options: Counsel the caregiver on positioning and attachment so that the infant can breastfeed better.
The infant is seriously ill if they are unable to feed. You must urgently refer.
Recommend that the caregiver give other safe fluids by cup.
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease and feeding lessons: not able to feed is a severe sign.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise A (young infants are special)
narrative: Try not to look back at the material.

questions.question: Young infants are up to 2 months of age.
Young infants have a different section of charts because they have a separate IMNCI process that is entirely different from the process for the sick child.
questions.explain: The process is the same; the charts are separate because some signs and symptoms are age-specific.

questions.question: Severe infections are the most serious illness in the first two months of life.
Young infants and children are very similar in how they show signs of illness.
questions.explain: Young infants show signs of illness very differently, so they are assessed for different signs and symptoms.

questions.question: Sami is 2 months old. He is considered a sick young infant.
questions.explain: At 2 months Sami is a sick child: young infants are up to 2 months.

questions.question: Tick the measures that are important care for young infants.
options: Skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care) to keep the infant warm
Give water regularly to keep infant hydrated
Seek care immediately if infant develops signs of serious illness
Change gowns before holding young infant
Give all immunizations at birth, and never again
Wash hands before handling the young infant
Rub the young infant with oils, lotion, or vaseline to keep skin moist

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise B (signs of serious illness)
narrative: Answer the questions about assessing for signs of serious illness.

questions.question: How many breaths per minute is fast breathing in a young infant?
How do you decide if an infant has fast breathing?
points: Make sure the infant is calm
Count the breaths in one minute
If 60 or more, count a second time to confirm

questions.question: How will you measure temperature in a young infant?
points: Axillary (armpit) temperature
Or feel the infant's abdomen or armpit
Rectal thresholds are about 0.5 °C higher

questions.question: What temperature is a fever in a young infant?
What temperature is low body temperature?
Chest indrawing is identified when an infant is breathing OUT.
questions.explain: It is seen when the infant breathes IN: the lower chest wall goes in instead of out.

questions.question: A healthy umbilicus is often red, and sometimes drains pus.
questions.explain: A red or draining umbilicus is a sign of infection.

questions.question: Any difficulty with feeding is an important issue for young infants.
Only severe chest indrawing is a serious sign in infants, as mild chest indrawing is normal in young infants.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise C (jaundice)
narrative: Answer the questions about assessing and classifying jaundice.

questions.question: Jaundice is a yellow discolouration of the skin.
Yellow soles and palms are normal in young infants.
questions.explain: Yellow palms and soles mean SEVERE JAUNDICE.

questions.question: Many babies may have jaundice in the first week of life, especially if they are low birth weight or premature.
Jaundice in a young infant less than 24 hours old is very serious.
To assess for jaundice of the skin, soles or palms, blanch the skin and look for discolouration.
It is best to look for jaundice indoors under a lamp.
questions.explain: Look in natural light.

questions.question: Jaundice that persists beyond 2 weeks requires further investigation.
Precious is 14 days old. Her skin is not discoloured. Her palms and soles are normal.
Kai was born last night, less than 24 hours ago. His skin is very yellow.
Sal is 2 weeks old. She has yellow discolouration of the skin and eyes. Her palms and soles are not yellow.
questions.explain: JAUNDICE. At 14 days or older she should also be referred for assessment.

questions.question: Biki is 21 days old. He has yellow skin, but his palms and soles are not yellow. How would you classify Biki? What would you do?
points: JAUNDICE (yellow)
He is older than 14 days: refer for assessment

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise D, Henri (6 hours)
narrative: Henri was born 6 hours ago at home. His weight is 3.0 kg. His axillary temperature is 36.5 °C. He is brought to the health facility because he did not cry immediately after birth and is having difficult breathing.
The health worker first checks the young infant for signs of very severe disease and local bacterial infection. The father says that the young infant has not had convulsions and has not yet been fed.

The health worker counts 74 breaths per minute. He repeats the count: the second count is 70 breaths per minute. He finds that the young infant has severe chest indrawing. The young infant moves only when he is stimulated. The umbilicus is normal, and there are no skin pustules.
There is no jaundice. Henri does not have diarrhoea.
learningPoints: Henri has fast breathing (counted twice), severe chest indrawing and moves only when stimulated: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red). He needs urgent referral.
exercises.explain: Henri has fast breathing (counted twice), severe chest indrawing and moves only when stimulated: POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE (red). He needs urgent referral.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise D, Sashi (1 week)
narrative: Sashi is 1 week old. Her weight is 3.4 kg. Her axillary temperature is 37 °C. Her caregiver brought her to the clinic because she has a rash.
The health worker assesses for signs of very severe disease and local bacterial infection. Sashi's caregiver says that there were no convulsions and that the infant is feeding well.

Sashi's breathing rate is 55 per minute. She has no chest indrawing. Her umbilicus is normal. The health worker examines her entire body and finds a red rash with a few skin pustules on her buttocks. She is awake and has spontaneous movements.
She has neither jaundice nor diarrhoea.
learningPoints: A few skin pustules with no sign of very severe disease: LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION (yellow). Treat at home and follow up in 2 days.
exercises.explain: A few skin pustules with no sign of very severe disease: LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION (yellow). Treat at home and follow up in 2 days.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Mimi, 6 weeks (the module case)
narrative: Biya brings her first child, Mimi, aged 6 weeks, on Tuesday morning. Since the weekend Mimi has not been taking the breast as often as usual, and Biya thinks she is getting worse. This is the first visit for this problem.
Mimi weighs 3.1 kg (birth weight 3.5 kg). Her axillary temperature is 34.7 °C.
Biya tries several times to put Mimi on the breast but Mimi does not attach at all. Biya says that she has had no convulsions.

You count 45 breaths per minute. Her lower chest wall moves in quite severely when she breathes in. She has no skin pustules. The umbilicus is not red or draining pus. When you move Mimi's arm to stimulate her, she drops the arm when you release it.
When you press Mimi's skin in natural light it is yellow, and her palms and soles are also yellow. Biya is not sure when the yellow colour first appeared.
learningPoints: Mimi has four signs of very severe disease (not feeding well, low body temperature, severe chest indrawing, reduced movement) and yellow palms and soles. Two red classifications: refer urgently after the first dose of ampicillin and gentamicin, preventing low blood sugar and keeping her warm.
exercises.explain: Mimi has four signs of very severe disease (not feeding well, low body temperature, severe chest indrawing, reduced movement) and yellow palms and soles. Two red classifications: refer urgently after the first dose of ampicillin and gentamicin, preventing low blood sugar and keeping her warm.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise E (treatment for Henri and Sashi)
narrative: Return to Henri's and Sashi's recording forms. Decide the treatments, using the young infant chart (Sudan national booklet doses). Write complete answers including the schedule and dose.

questions.question: Henri should be urgently referred.
questions.explain: He is classified POSSIBLE SERIOUS BACTERIAL INFECTION OR VERY SEVERE DISEASE.

questions.question: Henri is 6 hours old and weighs 3.0 kg. What pre-referral treatments does he need?
points: First dose of IM ampicillin 1.5 ml (250 mg/2.5 ml)
First dose of IM gentamicin 1.5 ml (10 mg/ml, under 7 days)
Treat to prevent low blood sugar (breastfeed, or 30 ml breast milk or sugar water, by tube if he cannot swallow)
Advise how to keep him warm on the way
Refer urgently
questions.explain: Sudan booklet doses. The WHO module gives ampicillin 1.0 ml and gentamicin 1.6 ml for its formulations.

questions.question: Sashi should be urgently referred.
questions.explain: Sashi has LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION and is treated at home.

questions.question: Sashi is 1 week old and weighs 3.4 kg. What treatments and advice does she need?
points: Oral amoxicillin 2.5 ml syrup (125 mg/5 ml) or ¼ tablet (250 mg) twice daily for 5 days; first dose in the clinic
Teach the caregiver to give it at home, with checking questions
Teach her to treat the pustules: wash hands, wash off pus and crusts with soap and water, dry, paint with gentian violet 0.5%, wash hands; twice daily for 5 days
Follow up in 2 days
Signs to return immediately
questions.explain: Sudan uses amoxicillin. The WHO module also allows co-trimoxazole 1.25 ml syrup twice daily.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise F (follow-up for Sashi)
narrative: Sashi, 1 week old, was classified LOCAL BACTERIAL INFECTION for skin pustules on her buttocks. Her caregiver gave the oral antibiotic and learned to clean the skin and apply gentian violet. She returns after 2 days with no new problems.

questions.question: How would you reassess Sashi?
points: Look at the skin pustules: are there many or severe pustules?
Are the redness and pus improved: fewer pustules, drying up?

questions.question: You see fewer pustules and less redness. What does Sashi need now?
options: Complete the 5 days of antibiotic, and continue cleaning and gentian violet for 5 days
Stop the antibiotic: she is better
questions.explain: She is improving, but must finish the 5 days of treatment.

narrative: Decide whether each sign shows good or poor attachment, then match each infant with how well they are suckling.

questions.question: Chin away from breast
More areola visible above than below mouth

Chin touching breast

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise J (immunizations)
narrative: Decide if the infant needs any immunizations today, and which ones, using the national schedule (birth: OPV 0, BCG; 6 weeks: OPV 1, Rota 1, PCV 1, Penta 1, IPV 1; 10 weeks: OPV 2, Rota 2, PCV 2, Penta 2).

questions.question: 16 days old, received BCG.
questions.explain: OPV 0 is not given after 14 days. Give the 6-week vaccines at 6 weeks.

questions.question: 7 weeks old, received Penta 1 (WHO: DPT-1 and Hib-1). What does the infant need today?
points: OPV 1
Rota 1, PCV 1 and IPV 1 if not given
Next appointment at 10 weeks
questions.explain: WHO answer: OPV 1 and hepatitis B 1. In Sudan, hepatitis B is part of Penta.

questions.question: 4 weeks old, received BCG and OPV 0.
8 weeks old, received BCG and OPV 0. The infant is being urgently referred today.
options: No vaccines now; refer urgently and note the vaccines due on the referral note
Give all the 6-week vaccines first, then refer

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise K (counselling on feeding)
narrative: Practise counselling a caregiver about infant feeding.

questions.question: Spoon feeding is not safe.
questions.explain: Spoon feeding is safe if the mother gives enough, though slower than a cup.

questions.question: Cup feeding is the preferred method of feeding (when an infant cannot breastfeed).
Bottle feeding is unsafe.
Cup feeding is preferred over spoon feeding.
Bottle feeding is most recommended for young infants to practise suckling.
Srilekha is unsure how to hold her infant while breastfeeding. How will you show her?
points: Head and body in line
Facing the breast, nose opposite the nipple
Held close to her body
Whole body supported, not just the neck and shoulders

questions.question: Yoonhee is unsure how to help her infant attach. What should she do?
points: Touch the infant's lips with her nipple
Wait until the mouth is opening wide
Move the infant quickly onto the breast, aiming the lower lip well below the nipple

questions.question: How often should a caregiver breastfeed in 24 hours?
Jaya breastfeeds but also gives her 4-month-old some watery porridge. What do you recommend?
points: Breastfeed more: on demand, at least 8 times in 24 hours
Stop the porridge and breastfeed exclusively
Find out why she began the porridge and what feeding difficulties she has

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Exercise L (home care for Sashi)
narrative: Use Sashi's case: local bacterial infection with pustules on her buttocks.

questions.question: List the steps the caregiver should take to treat the skin pustules at home.
points: Wash hands
Gently wash off pus and crusts with soap and water
Dry the area
Paint with gentian violet (0.5%)
Wash hands

questions.question: How often should she treat the pustules?
What are the 3 main points of home care for the young infant?
points: Breastfeed frequently, as often and as long as the infant wants, day and night
When to return
Keep the young infant warm at all times

questions.question: What would you tell Sashi's caregiver about when to return?
points: Follow-up in 2 days to check the pustules are improving
Return immediately if breastfeeding poorly, sicker, fever, fast or difficult breathing, feels cold, yellow palms and soles

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Review questions (post-test)
narrative: You have finished the module. Answer the same questions as in the pre-test and compare your scores.

questions.question: Why do young infants require different care than sick children?
options: Young infants are much quicker to recover from illness because they are young.
Young infants show signs of illness differently. They can also become ill and die from an infection very quickly.
Young infants very rarely get sick.
questions.explain: Introduction to the sick young infant: young infants are special.

questions.question: Which of the following is important care for a young infant?
options: Keeping the infant loosely bundled so he can begin to move his arms and legs
Keeping the umbilical cord moist so that it falls off quickly
Keeping the infant warm through skin-to-skin care
questions.explain: Introduction and infant care lessons: keep the infant warm; the cord is kept clean and dry.

questions.question: What are the feeding recommendations for sick young infants?
options: Exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding for at least 6 months
Breastfeeding and additional sources of fluid, like water, to hydrate
Soft complementary foods as soon as the child is ready
questions.explain: Feeding lessons: exclusive, on-demand breastfeeding. (The printed WHO answer key gives B, which contradicts the module text.)

questions.question: What are signs that a young infant is seriously ill and needs urgent referral and care?
options: Breathing more than 60 breaths per minute
Some jaundice, where the eyes are yellow but not the palms or soles
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease: fast breathing (60 or more, counted twice) is a sign of very severe disease. A few pustules are a local infection.

questions.question: A young infant presents at your clinic. The caregiver says the infant had been feeding well, but in the past 2 days is unable to breastfeed at all. What actions will you take?
options: Counsel the caregiver on positioning and attachment so that the infant can breastfeed better.
The infant is seriously ill if they are unable to feed. You must urgently refer.
Recommend that the caregiver give other safe fluids by cup.
questions.explain: Signs of serious disease and feeding lessons: not able to feed is a severe sign.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 2: Logbook assessment questions
narrative: Questions about the module. You may use your chart booklet, but not your study modules.

questions.question: In IMNCI, the sick young infant refers to:
Which of these is a sign of very severe disease in a young infant?
options: Chest indrawing, either mild or severe

questions.question: Which of these is a sign of local bacterial infection in a young infant?
options: 3 skin pustules on the infant's shoulder

questions.question: A 2-week-old has fast breathing if he is breathing:
options: 50 breaths per minute or more, counted twice
60 breaths or more per minute, and the same in a second count

questions.question: A 7-week-old classified with very severe disease:
options: Should be assessed for correct position and attachment for breastfeeding
Can improve at the clinic level and does not need urgent referral
Needs a first dose of IM antibiotics before urgent referral

questions.question: A 1-month-old with diarrhoea can be classified SEVERE DEHYDRATION if:
options: The child had very low weight for age
The child was lethargic even though there was no other sign of dehydration
The child had at least two signs of dehydration

questions.question: Thato is 14 days old. His palms appear yellow. How do you classify, and what will you do?
options: SEVERE JAUNDICE, treat Thato in the clinic
JAUNDICE, and refer if Thato returns after 1 week with jaundice

questions.question: An infant has good attachment if:
options: His lower lip is turned in and more areola is visible below than above the mouth
The chin is touching the breast and his lower lip is turned outward
More areola shows above the mouth and his mouth is narrow

questions.question: An infant may not suckle effectively if:
options: Her mouth is wide open when she is attached
She is taking slow, deep sucks
She has a blocked nose or is classified with very severe disease

questions.question: If an infant has a feeding problem, this could mean he is:
options: Not well attached, having less than 8 breastfeeds in 24 hours, or receiving other foods or drinks
Receiving only breast milk from the mother, and feeding on demand
Receiving expressed breast milk from a cup

questions.question: An infant who is 2 months old is a young infant.
A young infant brought to the clinic because of difficulty feeding can be treated by the clinic nurse.
questions.explain: Not feeding well is a sign of very severe disease: refer urgently.

questions.question: A young infant with cough or difficult breathing and severe chest indrawing is classified as SEVERE PNEUMONIA.
questions.explain: In the young infant, severe chest indrawing is a sign of very severe disease.

questions.question: If a young infant is brought in while convulsing, rush the baby to hospital and do not spend time giving treatments.
questions.explain: Give the pre-referral treatments (Sudan: manage the airway and give rectal diazepam; first dose of antibiotics) then refer.

questions.question: A young infant aged 6 weeks with jaundice may have a serious problem and needs to be referred to a hospital.
questions.explain: Jaundice at 14 days or older: refer for assessment (Sudan and WHO charts). The printed WHO key says FALSE: reviewer to confirm.

questions.question: A young infant with severe chest indrawing can be classified with very severe disease.
Umbilicus care and good hygiene are very important to keeping a young infant healthy.
One important sign of good attachment is that the infant's mouth is wide open.
You need to give the young infant water frequently to prevent dehydration.
questions.explain: Exclusive breastfeeding: no water.

questions.question: Skin-to-skin contact keeps an infant warm.
